items.metaDescription: Moneypenny, Poly.ai and Yellow.ai solve different problems. This guide maps each platform to the operational challenge it's built for, so you choose right.
items.body:
Most businesses comparing these three platforms are already asking the wrong question. The question is not which one is best. It is which one solves the problem you actually have.

Moneypenny, Poly.ai, and Yellow.ai occupy the same broad category in vendor shortlists and procurement conversations. In reality, they represent three fundamentally different operating philosophies: enterprise voice automation, omnichannel AI orchestration, and premium human-led service. Putting them in the same comparison is a bit like evaluating a logistics firm, a software platform, and a personal assistant against the same scorecard.

The most expensive mistake in customer communications is not choosing the wrong vendor. It is buying the wrong category of solution entirely.

The financial stakes are real. [AI can reduce the cost of routine customer interactions by 80 to 90%](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/ai-agent-vs-human-agent-cost) compared to human agents. But [between 85% and 93% of consumers still prefer a human agent](https://www.glean.com/perspectives/can-ai-agents-fully-replace-human-customer-support) when a conversation is complex, sensitive, or emotionally charged. Neither data point tells you what to do. They just confirm that the decision is more nuanced than a feature comparison will reveal.

This guide does something different. Rather than scoring platforms against each other, it maps each one to the operational problem it is actually built to solve. By the end, you will know which model fits your situation, and you will have a diagnostic framework to justify that decision internally.

Key Takeaways

Poly.ai, Yellow.ai, and Moneypenny are not interchangeable. They solve fundamentally different problems.

The AI break-even point sits at roughly 40,000 to 60,000 annual interactions. Below that, human or hybrid is often more cost-effective.

Gartner predicts 50% of organisations that planned AI-only service will abandon those plans by 2027.

The most common buying mistake is not choosing the wrong vendor. It is buying the wrong category of solution.

For most mid-market UK organisations, the right answer is a hybrid model. The question is how to design it.

Poly.ai: built for enterprises with high inbound call volume and complex telephony environments

Yellow.ai: built for organisations that want AI to orchestrate workflows across multiple channels and systems

Moneypenny: built for businesses where the quality of the first human interaction is a core part of the brand

The Economics of the Decision

Before evaluating any platform, it helps to understand why this market exists and why the dominant narrative around AI in customer service is already being revised.

The cost differential between human agents and AI is stark:

Human agents cost between £3.00 and £6.50 per minute of customer interaction, when salary, benefits, training, and infrastructure are factored in

AI virtual agents handle routine interactions at £0.03 to £0.25 per minute, representing an [80 to 90% reduction in cost](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/ai-agent-vs-human-agent-cost) for transactional tasks

The break-even point for AI implementation typically falls between 40,000 and 60,000 annual interactions, with [full payback often realised within four to six months](https://www.teneo.ai/blog/ai-vs-live-agent-cost-the-complete-2025-analysis-and-comparison-2)

AI deployed alongside human agents can increase human productivity by [up to 66%](https://www.billgosling.com/blog/ai-is-the-catalyst-for-smarter-and-humane-customer-service-in-2025/), freeing people for the conversations that require genuine judgement

The financial case for AI is compelling. But the more important data point is what is happening to organisations that went all-in on it.

Gartner predicts that by 2027, 50% of organisations that planned to drastically reduce their human customer service workforce in favour of AI will abandon those plans. The "agent-less" contact centre, it turns out, is a fundamentally flawed operational objective. ([Gartner, 2025](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-10-gartner-predicts-50-percent-of-organizations-will-abandon-plans-to-reduce-customer-service-workforce-due-to-ai))

The emerging consensus is a hybrid model: AI handles volume, triage, and routine resolution; humans handle escalations, sensitive conversations, and high-value relationships. The question is not whether to use AI. It is where AI belongs in your specific customer journey, and which platform is designed to fill that role.

Poly.ai: Built for the Phone Channel

If your primary problem is inbound call volume, long wait times, or an IVR system that frustrates callers, Poly.ai is the strongest fit of the three. It is not a general-purpose AI platform that happens to handle voice. It is built from the ground up for enterprise telephony, engineered specifically to handle natural telephone conversations at scale.

Where Poly.ai excels

Poly.ai's core technology is a proprietary Spoken Language Understanding stack combined with the ConveRT machine learning model, benchmarked as an industry leader for intent comprehension. Callers can speak naturally, use regional slang, and change direction mid-sentence without being forced into a numeric menu. The system corrects speech recognition errors in real time, filters background noise, and adapts to heavy regional accents.

The platform integrates natively with major enterprise telephony infrastructure, including Cisco, Genesys, Avaya, and Amazon Connect. That means it can modernise a legacy contact centre without requiring a full system replacement. It holds [SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and GDPR certifications](https://poly.ai/security), making it deployable in regulated sectors including healthcare, financial services, and utilities.

The ROI case studies are among the most compelling in the industry:

Pacific Gas and Electric managed 16 million annual calls with an outdated IVR. After deploying Poly.ai, it achieved a [67% call containment rate](https://poly.ai/customers/), saved 35,000 labour hours, and increased customer satisfaction scores on outage calls by 22%

The Melting Pot recovered £300,000 in previously lost after-hours revenue within six months, automating 68% of reservation-related calls

Côte Brasserie achieved a 76% conversion rate on calls that would have gone unanswered, automating 3,000 reservations per month

UniCredit automated 27% of banking calls, routed callers 83% faster, and saw a 14-point increase in Net Promoter Score within six months

The managed service model is a genuine differentiator for large enterprises. Poly.ai handles conversational design, API integration, deployment testing, and post-launch optimisation. Internal teams do not need dedicated machine learning engineers or dialogue scientists.

Where Poly.ai struggles

The managed service model is also where the trade-offs begin. There is no self-serve visual builder or no-code interface. Changes to conversational flows, prompt modifications, and workflow updates go through Poly.ai's account management and engineering teams. For agile marketing or IT departments that want to iterate quickly, this creates bottlenecks.

Pricing is custom-quoted based on call volume and integration complexity. There is no public pricing, no free trial, and no accessible entry point for mid-market businesses. This is an enterprise platform with an enterprise price tag.

Analytics dashboards are also more limited than competing omnichannel platforms, offering less self-serve granularity for teams that want to interrogate their own data.

Choose Poly.ai if: your primary service channel is the phone, inbound call volumes are high and often unpredictable, and your biggest operational opportunity is reducing friction and cost on telephony without rebuilding your entire contact centre infrastructure.

Yellow.ai: Built for Orchestration Across Channels

Yellow.ai solves a different problem. Where Poly.ai is designed to answer the phone better, Yellow.ai is designed to complete the process. It is an omnichannel agentic AI platform built for organisations that want automation to span web chat, WhatsApp, SMS, email, voice, and back-end business systems, all from a single platform. If you are evaluating whether your current setup can support that kind of connected experience, Fortay's [omnichannel CX self-assessment](https://fortayconnect.com/content/how-to-improve-omnichannel-customer-experience) is a useful starting point.

The distinction matters. A customer querying an order via WhatsApp, triggering a Salesforce record update, cross-referencing inventory in SAP, and receiving a refund confirmation in the same conversation, that is a Yellow.ai use case. It is not a Poly.ai use case, and it is certainly not a Moneypenny one.

Where Yellow.ai excels

The platform's technical architecture is genuinely sophisticated. It runs on a multi-LLM framework using over 15 large language models, underpinned by an Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that connects directly to enterprise data sources including SharePoint, Salesforce, Zendesk, AWS S3, and SAP. Rather than matching keywords to scripted responses, it reasons across live data to generate contextually accurate answers in real time.

Yellow.ai uses a hierarchical agent structure: a "Super Agent" orchestrates multiple specialist "Domain Agents". This maintains conversational memory even when users change the subject mid-interaction. Yellow.ai's recently launched Nexus platform extends this further, operating autonomously above the enterprise technology stack and [reporting a 98.9% success rate](https://yellow.ai/platform/) across autonomous workflow executions.

The scale of reach is significant:

35+ native communication channels, including WhatsApp, web chat, SMS, email, and voice assistants

135+ languages supported natively

150+ pre-built integrations with enterprise platforms including Salesforce, SAP, Oracle, ServiceNow, and Shopify

20+ analytics dashboards for tracking sentiment, automation rates, drop-off points, and topic clustering

A no-code visual builder and "Ask AI" prompt interface allow business users to construct workflows without writing code, and a free tier (capped at 500 monthly sessions) provides a low-risk entry point for evaluation.

Where Yellow.ai struggles

The "no-code" positioning requires qualification. Simple workflows are genuinely accessible. But complex multi-system integrations, API data exchanges, and enterprise-grade logic flows require significant technical ownership. Teams without dedicated IT resource or systems integration capability consistently report delayed deployments and ongoing maintenance overhead.

User feedback on enterprise review platforms reflects a clear split. Developers and enterprise architects rate the platform highly for its depth and versatility. Business users flag inconsistent support outside premium tiers, occasional interface performance issues, and pricing that becomes difficult to forecast as volumes grow. The usage-based enterprise pricing model scales with volume, which is appealing in principle but creates budget uncertainty for rapidly growing businesses.

For organisations seeking simple, single-channel automation, Yellow.ai is over-engineered and cost-inefficient. Its value is realised when the ambition matches the architecture.

Choose Yellow.ai if: your goal is AI-led workflow automation across multiple channels and systems, you have the internal technical capability to configure and maintain complex logic flows, and you want a single platform to centralise your entire digital customer and employee experience.

Moneypenny: Built for the Interaction Itself

Moneypenny operates on a different premise entirely. Its core proposition is not automation. It is that the quality of the first human interaction is a brand asset, not just a service function, and that for certain businesses, no AI system can replicate what a skilled, knowledgeable human receptionist delivers in those first thirty seconds.

That is not a sentimental position. It is a commercially grounded one. [Around 63% of customers say they do not believe AI can ever fully replace humans in customer service](https://www.glean.com/perspectives/can-ai-agents-fully-replace-human-customer-support), and nearly 50% say they would switch providers if subjected to AI-driven support without a clear human escalation path. For legal firms, private healthcare practices, premium real estate agencies, and financial services businesses, the first call is often a new client, a distressed patient, or a sensitive case. Getting that interaction wrong has consequences that extend well beyond a poor CSAT score.

Where Moneypenny excels

Moneypenny assigns named, dedicated receptionists to each client. Those agents become familiar with the business's specific brand tone, VIP contacts, ongoing campaigns, and operational priorities. This is not a call centre model with a rotating pool of agents reading from a script. It functions as an extension of the in-house team.

Human agents bring capabilities that AI cannot yet reliably replicate: reading emotional tone in real time, de-escalating difficult conversations through genuine empathy, and making adaptive judgements when a situation does not fit any predefined workflow. Trustpilot reviews for Moneypenny consistently highlight the professionalism and attentiveness of its staff, reflecting a service that delivers on its premium positioning.

Moneypenny has also responded to the AI era rather than ignoring it. Its hybrid model uses AI as a triage layer, handling authentication, basic data capture, and routine enquiries, before executing a warm transfer to a human receptionist for anything that warrants it. This approach preserves the human touch where it matters while reducing cost and wait times on routine interactions.

Where Moneypenny struggles

The cost structure is the primary constraint. Base plans start at around £165 per month for human answering and £99 per month for AI answering, but these figures rarely reflect the real cost of operation for an active business. Overage charges of £1.65 per call apply the moment a client exceeds their plan allowance. One-time setup fees can reach £1,000. Businesses requiring full 24/7 coverage face additional costs that can push monthly spend to £300 to £400 or more.

Scalability is the other hard limit. Unlike cloud-native AI platforms that absorb call spikes instantly, a human-staffed service has physical capacity constraints. A sudden surge in inbound enquiries, triggered by a marketing campaign or a media mention, will create queuing and delay that an AI system would handle without friction.

Choose Moneypenny if: your brand depends on the quality of human interaction, your callers are often in high-stakes or emotionally sensitive situations, and you cannot afford for the first point of contact to feel transactional or impersonal.

Side-by-Side: How the Three Platforms Compare

The tables below consolidate the key structural differences and flag the most common mismatches Fortay sees in practice.

Platform overview

|  |  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
|  | Poly.ai | Yellow.ai | Moneypenny |
| Primary use case | Enterprise voice automation | Omnichannel AI orchestration | Premium human answering |
| Core technology | Proprietary SLU, ConveRT model | Agentic RAG, 15+ LLMs, Nexus | Human agents + CRM integration |
| Deployment model | Fully managed (vendor-led) | Self-serve / low-code platform | Managed outsourced service |
| Pricing structure | Custom enterprise quote | Usage-based (free tier available) | Tiered base + per-call overages |
| Scalability | Instant, unlimited | Instant, unlimited | Limited by human staffing capacity |
| Implementation time | Weeks to months | Days to weeks | Days |
| Internal overhead | Very low | Moderate to high | Very low |
| Compliance | SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR | SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR | PCI compliant |
| Best-fit sectors | Utilities, hospitality, banking, healthcare | eCommerce, digital-native, IT-heavy organisations | Legal, healthcare, property, financial services |

The three most common buying mistakes

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
| Mistake | What happens | The right fit instead |
| Buying Yellow.ai when the problem is call volume | Teams spend months configuring omnichannel workflows when the core issue is unanswered or poorly handled phone calls | Poly.ai, or a hybrid model with Moneypenny |
| Buying Moneypenny when the problem is scale | Human-led service becomes cost-prohibitive as interaction volume grows; overages erode the ROI case | Poly.ai for voice volume; Yellow.ai for multi-channel volume |
| Buying Poly.ai when the problem spans multiple channels | Voice containment improves, but digital touchpoints remain unconnected and the customer experience is fragmented | Yellow.ai for full omnichannel orchestration |

How to Choose: A Diagnostic Framework

The right platform becomes obvious once you have answered the right questions. Start with the operational problem, not the vendor shortlist.

Ask yourself these three questions first:

What is your primary customer channel? If the majority of your inbound contact arrives by phone, voice automation is the priority. If it is distributed across web, messaging apps, and email, omnichannel orchestration is the more pressing need. If it is predominantly phone-based and the quality of that call is central to your brand, human-led service is likely the right anchor.

What is your annual interaction volume? The AI break-even threshold sits at roughly 40,000 to 60,000 interactions per year. Below that level, the ROI case for a platform like Poly.ai is harder to make; a hybrid model anchored by Moneypenny is often more cost-effective. Above that threshold, AI automation typically pays back within four to six months.

How sensitive are your conversations? Routine, predictable, transactional enquiries are ideal for AI containment. Emotionally charged, high-value, or legally sensitive conversations carry a different cost of failure. If getting those interactions wrong has direct revenue or reputational consequences, the human element is not a cost to be optimised away; it is part of the product.

The hybrid question

For most mid-market UK organisations, the honest answer is that no single platform covers every scenario. The real decision is how to design the right combination: which interactions should be automated, which should be human-led, and where the handoff between the two should occur.

Gartner's prediction that half of organisations will walk back their AI-only ambitions by 2027 is a useful anchor here. The hybrid model is not a compromise; it is the operationally sound approach for businesses that serve a mix of routine and high-stakes interactions.

One practical note on Yellow.ai specifically: the no-code positioning is genuine for simple use cases, but if your workflows require deep CRM integration or multi-system logic, budget for internal technical resource to configure and maintain them. Underestimating that overhead is the most common reason Yellow.ai deployments underperform.

The Fortay View

The platforms in this comparison are genuinely good at what they are built for. The problem is that most businesses arrive at the vendor conversation before they have properly diagnosed what they are trying to fix.

In practice, Fortay sees three buying mistakes repeat themselves across organisations of every size.

The first is buying a workflow platform when the real problem is call handling. Yellow.ai is a powerful platform, but organisations that choose it because it appeared on a "best AI customer service" list, without first confirming that multi-channel orchestration is actually their constraint, consistently find themselves in a lengthy, expensive configuration process that solves the wrong problem.

The second is buying a premium human answering service when the real need is scale. Moneypenny is the right choice for specific interaction types and sectors. But when the underlying problem is volume, and the business is processing tens of thousands of routine enquiries, the per-call cost model becomes unsustainable quickly. The solution is not a better human service; it is a different architecture.

The third is buying voice AI when the problem spans multiple channels. Poly.ai will transform telephony performance. But if a significant portion of customer contact arrives via web chat, WhatsApp, or email, improving call containment addresses only part of the picture.

The right question in every case is the same: what is the actual operational failure, and which model is designed to fix it?

Fortay's role in this process is to map the problem before recommending a solution. That means working through interaction volumes, channel mix, conversation sensitivity, and internal technical capability before a vendor is introduced. Our [CX and AI advisory service](https://fortayconnect.com/advisory) is designed specifically for this diagnostic phase. Technology selection without that diagnostic step is how businesses end up with the wrong platform, at the wrong cost, solving the wrong problem.

The decision becomes straightforward when you start with the diagnosis.

Conclusion

There is no universal winner in this comparison, because each platform is optimised for a different operating model. Poly.ai, Yellow.ai, and Moneypenny are each genuinely excellent at the problem they are designed to solve.

The takeaway is the framework, not the ranking. Diagnose the operational problem first. Match the solution to the problem, not to the feature list.

If you are working through this decision and are unsure which model fits your customer journeys, service pressures, and internal capability, that is precisely the kind of question Fortay exists to help answer. You can explore how we approach [contact centre CX transformation](https://fortayconnect.com/cx-contact-center) or speak directly with our team.

FAQs

What is the main difference between Moneypenny, Poly.ai and Yellow.ai?

They solve different problems. Poly.ai is built for enterprise voice automation on high-volume phone channels. Yellow.ai orchestrates AI workflows across multiple digital channels and back-end systems. Moneypenny provides premium human-led answering for businesses where interaction quality is a core brand value.

Which platform is best for a mid-market UK business?

It depends on your primary channel, interaction volume, and conversation sensitivity. Below 40,000 to 60,000 annual interactions, a hybrid model anchored by Moneypenny is often more cost-effective than full AI deployment. Above that threshold, Poly.ai or Yellow.ai typically deliver ROI within four to six months.

Is Poly.ai suitable for small or mid-sized businesses?

Generally no. Poly.ai is priced and structured for large enterprises with high inbound call volumes. There is no public pricing, no free trial, and no self-serve interface. Mid-market businesses with moderate call volumes are likely better served by Moneypenny or a lighter AI solution.

How much does Moneypenny actually cost?

Base plans start at around £165 per month for human answering and £99 for AI answering. However, overage charges of £1.65 per call, setup fees of up to £1,000, and 24/7 coverage requirements mean real monthly costs for active businesses typically reach £300 to £400 or more.

Can Yellow.ai be used without a technical team?

Simple workflows are accessible via the no-code visual builder. However, complex multi-system integrations and enterprise-grade logic flows require significant technical ownership. Teams without dedicated IT or systems integration resource consistently report delayed deployments and ongoing maintenance overhead.

What is the hybrid model and which businesses should use it?

A hybrid model uses AI to handle routine, high-volume interactions and routes complex or sensitive conversations to human agents. Gartner predicts 50% of organisations that planned AI-only service will abandon those plans by 2027. For most mid-market UK organisations, hybrid is the operationally sound default.

items.metaDescription: Choose a CCaaS partner with less risk. Use these 7 board-level questions to test outcomes, integration, migration, compliance, and accountability.
items.body:
Most CCaaS buying processes are structured around the wrong things. Buyers spend weeks in product demos, comparing feature matrices and pricing tiers, while the questions that actually determine success, including how the migration will be managed, whether the platform integrates cleanly with existing systems, and who is accountable when things go wrong after go-live, go largely unasked.

The data on this is stark. [Research cited by Forrester](https://www.inflectioncx.com/intelligence/guides/ccaas-migration-guide) found that over 40% of CCaaS migrations have been unsuccessful, and only one in four decision-makers report being completely satisfied with their migration outcome. More than 80% of respondents said their new CCaaS solution had less functionality, robustness, and usability than the system it replaced. These are not outliers. They represent the predictable result of a buying process that prioritises demos over due diligence.

The real cost of a poor CCaaS decision is not just technical. It is operational disruption, damaged customer relationships, and a reputational risk that lands squarely on the executive who signed off on the investment.

For UK mid-market organisations, the stakes are particularly high. [According to MaxContact's 2025 UK customer experience research](https://www.maxcontact.com/articles/what-uk-customers-really-want-from-contact-centres-in-2025), 42% of consumers have already switched providers because of poor contact centre experiences, and 55% abandon calls when wait times become excessive. A platform transition that introduces even temporary service degradation carries direct commercial consequences.

The seven questions below are designed to reframe the CCaaS selection process around the dimensions that matter most to board-level decision makers: business outcomes, integration fit, AI readiness, migration capability, commercial structure, compliance posture, and post-launch accountability. They are not a replacement for a full RFP process, but they are the questions that separate vendors worth shortlisting from those that present well in demos and underdeliver in production.

Key takeaway: The right CCaaS partner is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that reduces execution risk, protects customer experience during change, and gets your business to value faster.

Question 1: What business outcomes are you committing to, and how will you measure them?

This is the question most vendors are not prepared to answer with specificity, and that tells you something important.

A credible CCaaS partner should be able to articulate what success looks like in measurable terms: first contact resolution rates, average handling time, customer satisfaction scores, cost per interaction, or agent utilisation. They should also be willing to tie those outcomes to a realistic timeline and explain what they need from your organisation to achieve them.

Vendors who respond with generic commitments about "improving customer experience" or "driving operational efficiency" without attaching metrics are signalling that accountability ends at the point of sale.

What to look for in the answer:

Specific KPIs referenced against your current baseline, not industry averages

A clear distinction between what the platform enables and what requires configuration, change management, or third-party support to achieve

Willingness to discuss what happens commercially if agreed outcomes are not met

Reference to a structured value realisation framework, not just an implementation plan

Why this matters for the board: CCaaS investments are increasingly scrutinised at CFO and CEO level. A partner who cannot articulate the business case in outcome terms will leave your leadership team defending a technology decision with no performance anchor.

Question 2: How does your platform integrate with our existing CRM, data, and operational systems?

Integration failure is one of the most consistent and costly sources of post-go-live disappointment in CCaaS deployments. When customer data is fragmented across disconnected systems, agents work with incomplete information, AI outputs become unreliable, and the unified customer experience promised in the sales process fails to materialise.

[According to the Puzzel State of Contact Centres 2026 report](https://www.cxtoday.com/contact-center/contact-center-industry-reports-2026/), only 3% of contact centres operate on a single unified platform. The average organisation manages 3.9 different contact centre technologies, and half of CX leaders say this fragmentation directly increases maintenance and support costs. Many businesses arrive at a CCaaS shortlist already carrying significant integration debt.

The critical question is not whether a vendor claims to integrate with your CRM. It is how that integration works in practice, who owns it technically, and what happens when it breaks.

What to look for in the answer:

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
| Integration dimension | Strong answer | Warning sign |
| CRM connectivity | Pre-built, tested connector with named CRM version | "We can build that" or vague API reference |
| Data residency | UK-based data storage confirmed, GDPR-compliant by design | Data sovereignty answered only on request |
| Legacy system coexistence | Documented approach to running old and new systems in parallel | Assumes clean cutover from day one |
| Ongoing integration support | Named owner and SLA for integration issues post-go-live | Handed to your IT team after implementation |

Why this matters for the CIO: Brittle integrations do not fail during demos. They fail during peak trading periods, compliance audits, and system updates. The CIO's accountability extends beyond the go-live date, and the integration model determines whether that accountability is manageable.

Question 3: How AI-ready is your platform, and what does that actually require from us?

AI capability has become a standard claim in every CCaaS pitch. The more useful question is what AI readiness actually demands from your organisation, and whether your current data, governance, and talent position can support it.

[Puzzel's 2026 data](https://www.cxtoday.com/contact-center/contact-center-industry-reports-2026/) reveals a telling gap: while 85% of CX leaders say their organisation is prepared to implement AI, only 34% feel fully prepared to execute at scale. The most common barriers are lack of internal AI expertise, data privacy and compliance concerns, and integration complexity. These are not platform limitations. They are organisational readiness gaps that no CCaaS vendor can solve on your behalf.

The practical risk is that AI layered onto fragmented or poorly governed data produces weaker outcomes, not better ones. Automated routing built on incomplete customer records, sentiment analysis trained on unrepresentative interaction data, and self-service journeys that cannot access real-time account information all create experiences that erode rather than build customer confidence.

What to look for in the answer:

A clear explanation of what data inputs the AI features require, and in what format

Transparency about which AI capabilities are native to the platform versus third-party integrations that add cost and complexity

A realistic assessment of the internal governance and data quality work required before AI features deliver value

Evidence of AI deployment at similar scale and sector, not just reference to a roadmap

A sharper test: Ask the vendor to walk you through a specific AI use case relevant to your operation, such as reducing repeat contact or improving first contact resolution, and to explain exactly what your organisation needs to provide to make it work. Vague answers here are a reliable predictor of post-go-live disappointment.

[MaxContact's UK research](https://www.maxcontact.com/articles/what-uk-customers-really-want-from-contact-centres-in-2025) is a useful grounding point: 70% of consumers still want to speak to a real person for complex issues. AI readiness matters, but it must be designed around human-assisted journeys, not in place of them.

Question 4: What does your migration methodology look like, and what is your track record?

Migration is where CCaaS decisions succeed or fail in practice. It is also the area most consistently underweighted in the buying process, because vendors have strong commercial incentives to minimise its complexity during the sales cycle.

The Forrester data referenced earlier is worth revisiting here. The top three obstacles to successful CCaaS migration are limited internal talent with new technology (cited by 42% of respondents), complex internal IT landscapes (38%), and lack of executive support (34%). None of these are platform problems. They are implementation and change management problems, and they are the vendor's responsibility to anticipate and mitigate, not yours to discover after contract signature.

[Gartner's broader data migration research](https://www.inflectioncx.com/intelligence/guides/ccaas-migration-guide) reinforces the scale of the risk: 83% of data migration projects either fail or exceed their budgets and schedules, with cost overruns averaging 30% and time overruns averaging 41%.

What a credible migration methodology includes

A partner with genuine migration capability should be able to provide:

A phased migration plan with defined stages, go/no-go criteria at each checkpoint, and a documented rollback strategy. Industry guidance recommends keeping the legacy system operational for two to four weeks post-cutover as a fallback.

A realistic timeline calibrated to your operation size. For contact centres with 100 to 500 agents, expect three to six months. Vendors who quote shorter timelines without qualifying assumptions are compressing the risk, not eliminating it.

Named migration resources rather than generic references to an implementation team. Who specifically will manage your migration, what is their experience, and how many concurrent migrations are they running?

Reference customers at comparable scale who have completed migration, not just those mid-implementation.

The question beneath the question

The real test is not whether the vendor has a migration methodology. It is whether they have migrated organisations of your size, complexity, and sector before, and whether they will let you speak to the people who led those programmes. If the answer to the latter is a curated reference list with pre-approved talking points, treat that as a risk signal.

Question 5: How is the commercial model structured, and what are the total costs over three years?

CCaaS pricing is rarely as straightforward as the initial proposal suggests. Seat-based licensing, consumption-based AI add-ons, integration fees, professional services, and support tiers each contribute to a total cost of ownership that can diverge significantly from the headline figure presented during the sales process.

The [CX Foundation's 2026 CCaaS buyer guidance](https://cxfoundation.com/blog/ccaas-providers) identifies pricing flexibility as one of the top evaluation criteria for decision makers, alongside AI integration, CRM convergence, and migration support. The shift towards consumption-based AI pricing in particular is creating new cost unpredictability for organisations that adopt AI features without modelling usage volumes carefully.

The questions to ask on commercial structure:

What is included in the base licence, and what triggers additional charges?

How are AI features priced: per seat, per interaction, per token, or as a bundle?

What are the integration and professional services costs, and are they fixed or variable?

What does the support model cost at each tier, and what response times are contractually guaranteed?

What are the exit provisions, data portability terms, and contract break clauses?

A practical framing for the board: Request a three-year total cost of ownership model that includes implementation, integration, training, ongoing support, and anticipated AI usage costs. Then stress-test it against two scenarios: one where adoption goes to plan, and one where you need to extend the migration timeline or add integration work mid-programme. The gap between those two scenarios is your financial exposure.

The hidden cost most buyers miss: Organisations that underestimate the internal resource burden of a CCaaS migration often absorb significant unplanned costs in IT time, agent retraining, and operational management during the transition period. A vendor who cannot help you model these costs is not yet treating you as a serious commercial partner.

Question 6: How does your platform address UK compliance obligations, and where does your data reside?

Compliance is not a secondary consideration to be resolved during implementation. For UK mid-market organisations, the regulatory environment around customer data is active and consequential, and it needs to be addressed at the point of vendor selection.

The [CCMA Contact Centre Technology Report 2026](https://www.ccma.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Contact-Centre-Technology-Report-2026.pdf) highlights growing concern across UK contact centres about GDPR exposure and the emerging implications of the EU AI Act for AI-assisted customer interactions. The ICO's enforcement posture has sharpened, and organisations processing customer data through cloud platforms face specific obligations around data residency, access controls, and audit trail integrity.

For any CCaaS platform handling customer voice, digital interaction, or payment data, the compliance questions are not optional.

Compliance dimensions to validate before shortlisting

UK GDPR and data residency: Is customer data stored on UK or EU servers? Can this be confirmed in writing and reflected in the Data Processing Agreement?

PCI-DSS scope: If agents handle card payments, how does the platform reduce or eliminate PCI scope? What certifications does the vendor hold?

ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials: Does the vendor hold current certification, and is it independently audited?

AI governance: For AI-assisted interactions, who is the data controller? How are AI model training data and outputs governed under UK GDPR?

Audit and access controls: Can the platform provide role-based access controls, complete interaction audit trails, and data subject access request support?

The question that reveals the most: Ask the vendor to provide their Data Processing Agreement and standard security documentation before the final shortlist stage. A vendor who is reluctant to share these documents before contract signature is one whose compliance posture deserves closer scrutiny.

Question 7: Who is accountable after go-live, and what does ongoing support look like in practice?

The post-go-live period is where CCaaS partnerships most frequently deteriorate. The sales team moves on, the implementation team closes out the project, and the organisation discovers that the support model it assumed it was buying is materially different from what the contract actually provides.

This is not an abstract risk. It is one of the most commonly reported sources of dissatisfaction in CCaaS deployments, and it is entirely preventable if the right questions are asked before contracts are signed.

What accountability looks like in a credible partner:

A named customer success manager or account director with defined responsibilities, not a shared inbox or ticketing system

A clear escalation path for operational issues, with contractually defined response times at each severity level

Regular business reviews that assess platform performance against the outcomes agreed at the outset, not just uptime and ticket resolution rates

A roadmap commitment that includes your organisation's specific requirements, not just a generic product update schedule

Transparency about how support is resourced: is it in-house, offshore, or managed through a third-party service partner?

The question that exposes the gap: Ask the vendor to describe the last time a customer raised a serious post-go-live issue and how it was resolved. A partner with genuine accountability will answer this with specificity. A vendor whose support model is weaker than their sales process will deflect or generalise.

Why this matters at CEO level: [CX Network's 2026 research](https://www.cxnetwork.com/) found that 83% of UK CX leaders see customer experience as a competitive differentiator. A CCaaS platform that works well in the first three months but degrades in performance over the following year creates a strategic liability, not a competitive advantage. Post-launch accountability is not a support question. It is a strategic one.

The Shortlist Checklist: Applying the Seven Questions

The seven questions above map directly to the dimensions most likely to determine whether a CCaaS investment delivers its intended value. The table below provides a summary reference for use during vendor evaluation and internal governance discussions.

|  |  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| # | Question | Primary stakeholder | Key risk if skipped |
| 1 | What outcomes are you committing to? | CEO / CX Director | No performance anchor; accountability ends at contract |
| 2 | How does integration work in practice? | CIO / IT Director | Brittle connections, data silos, AI underperformance |
| 3 | What does AI readiness require from us? | CX Director / CIO | AI features deployed before data or governance is ready |
| 4 | What is your migration methodology? | Operations / IT | Timeline overrun, service disruption, cost exposure |
| 5 | What are the total costs over three years? | CEO / Finance | Unexpected charges, underestimated internal burden |
| 6 | How do you address UK compliance? | CIO / Legal | GDPR exposure, ICO risk, data residency uncertainty |
| 7 | Who is accountable after go-live? | CEO / CX Director | Support degradation, no escalation path, strategic drift |

How to use this framework

These questions are most effective when asked in a structured vendor session rather than embedded in a generic RFP. The quality of the answer matters as much as the content: vendors who respond with specificity, reference comparable deployments, and acknowledge complexity are demonstrating the kind of commercial maturity that predicts a successful long-term partnership.

Vendors who deflect, generalise, or redirect to product features are telling you something important about how they will behave when the implementation gets difficult.

The standard to hold: A credible CCaaS partner should be able to answer all seven questions in detail before you reach the contract stage. If significant gaps remain at that point, the risk belongs to your organisation, not theirs.

For UK mid-market organisations evaluating CCaaS partners, the selection process is one of the highest-stakes technology decisions of the next three years. The [Fortay Connect advisory team](https://app.searchable.com/advisory) works with CX and operations leaders to stress-test vendor shortlists, validate integration and migration claims, and build the commercial frameworks needed to hold partners accountable from day one. If you are at shortlist stage and want an independent perspective, [speak to our team](https://app.searchable.com/cx-contact-center).

FAQs

What should a CCaaS buyer ask before choosing a partner?

Start with outcomes, integration, migration, compliance, commercial model, AI readiness, and post-go-live accountability. Those seven areas expose whether a vendor can deliver in production, not just perform well in a demo.

Why do CCaaS migrations fail so often?

They often fail because buyers under-scope migration work, overestimate internal capacity, or choose partners without enough implementation depth. Limited talent, complex IT estates, and weak executive alignment are common causes of delay and disruption.

How do you compare CCaaS partners beyond feature lists?

Compare them on business outcomes, CRM and data integration, migration method, support model, and total three-year cost. A stronger answer is specific, measurable, and tied to your current operating reality.

Why does compliance matter in CCaaS selection?

CCaaS platforms handle customer data, call recordings, and sometimes payment information, so UK GDPR, data residency, access control, and audit trail requirements all affect risk. Compliance should be validated before shortlist, not left until implementation.

items.metaDescription: Consumer Duty, SM\&CR, vulnerable customer detection - what a genuinely FCA-compliant AI contact centre requires in practice, and where most firms go wrong.
items.body:
Fortay Connect works with UK financial services firms to design and deploy AI [contact centre solutions](/cx-contact-center) that are built for FCA compliance from day one - not retrofitted to it. If you are planning an AI deployment or reviewing your current setup, get in touch to discuss your requirements.

Key Takeaways

The FCA applies Consumer Duty, SM\&CR, and Principles 6 and 7 to AI contact centre interactions. There is no bespoke AI regulation.

A named Senior Manager must own AI risk. Personal liability under SM\&CR extends to AI outputs.

Every AI interaction must be logged, retrievable, and mappable to a good customer outcome.

Vulnerable customer detection and escalation protocols must be built into the AI layer, not added afterwards.

AI models drift. Scheduled bias and accuracy audits are a compliance requirement, not a best practice.

Governance design comes before technology selection. Always.

Every financial services firm in the UK knows AI is coming to the contact centre. Most are already piloting it. But there is a question that keeps surfacing in boardrooms and compliance meetings that almost nobody is answering clearly: what does a contact centre that uses AI and stays on the right side of the FCA actually look like in practice?

This is not an abstract question. The [FCA's Consumer Duty](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/consumer-duty), which came into full force in July 2023, requires firms to demonstrate with evidence that their customer service delivers good outcomes. The [Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM\&CR)](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/senior-managers-certification-regime) means individual executives carry personal liability for AI failures. And the FCA has confirmed it will not create bespoke AI regulations; instead, it is applying existing frameworks harder.

The result is a compliance environment that is demanding, ambiguous, and increasingly scrutinised. Getting it right is not just a technology problem. It is a governance, process, and accountability problem.

The core principle: the FCA does not care whether a human or an AI handled the interaction. It cares whether the outcome for the customer was good and whether the firm can prove it.

An [FCA-compliant AI contact centre](https://www.fortayconnect.com/cx-contact-center) is entirely achievable. But it looks quite different from a standard AI deployment, and understanding those differences is the starting point for getting it right.

The Regulatory Frameworks That Apply

The FCA does not publish a checklist for AI contact centres. What it does publish and enforce are outcome-based frameworks that apply regardless of which technology a firm uses. Three are most directly relevant.

Consumer Duty

[Consumer Duty](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/consumer-duty) requires firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers across four areas: products and services, price and value, consumer understanding, and consumer support. For AI in the contact centre, the consumer support outcome is the most immediately relevant. Firms must be able to show that their AI-assisted or AI-led interactions actually help customers, not just that the technology is deployed.

SM\&CR Personal Accountability

Under [SM\&CR](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/senior-managers-certification-regime), a named Senior Manager must be accountable for each material risk area, including technology risk. When AI is deployed in a customer-facing context, that accountability extends to the AI's decisions and outputs. If an AI system gives incorrect information, handles a vulnerable customer inappropriately, or produces a biased outcome, a Senior Manager is personally in the frame.

FCA Principles for Businesses

[Principle 6](https://www.handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/PRIN/2/1.html) (treating customers fairly) and Principle 7 (communications must be clear, fair, and not misleading) apply directly to AI-generated customer interactions. An AI that produces confusing, incomplete, or misleading responses is a regulatory liability, not just a customer experience problem.

What an FCA-Compliant AI Contact Centre Actually Looks Like

Compliance is not a feature you switch on. It is built into the architecture, governance, and processes surrounding the AI. Here is what that looks like in practice across the five areas that matter most.

1\. A Named Accountability Owner

Every AI system deployed in a customer-facing context needs a named Senior Manager who owns the risk. This is not just a box-ticking exercise. It means that person has visibility of how the AI is performing, receives escalations when it fails, and can demonstrate to the FCA that oversight is active and documented.

2\. Full Interaction Logging and Audit Trails

An FCA-compliant AI contact centre records and retains every AI-assisted or AI-led customer interaction in a retrievable format. This is not optional. It is the evidence base for demonstrating good outcomes under Consumer Duty. Firms must be able to pull any interaction, review what the AI said or did, and show how it maps to the required outcome.

Key requirements for compliant interaction logging:

All AI-generated responses stored with timestamps

Escalation points (where AI handed off to a human) clearly flagged

[Sentiment and outcome data captured at interaction close](/content/benefits-cx-platform-managing-customer-expectations)

Retention periods aligned to FCA record-keeping requirements (typically 5-7 years for regulated activities)

3\. Vulnerable Customer Detection and Escalation

The FCA's [guidance on vulnerable customers](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/finalised-guidance/guidance-firms-fair-treatment-vulnerable-customers) is explicit: firms must identify vulnerability and respond appropriately. An AI that cannot detect signs of vulnerability, such as distress, confusion, bereavement, or financial difficulty, and escalate to a human agent is not FCA-compliant, regardless of how well it handles standard interactions.

Compliant AI contact centres build vulnerability detection into the AI layer itself, with defined escalation triggers and human handoff protocols that are tested and documented.

4\. Explainable Decisions and No Black Boxes

If the FCA asks why a customer received a particular response, or why an AI routed a complaint in a specific way, the firm must be able to answer. AI systems that operate as black boxes, producing outputs without traceable reasoning, are incompatible with the FCA's expectations around accountability and explainability.

This does not mean every AI decision needs a written rationale. It means the system architecture must allow compliance teams to reconstruct decision logic when required.

5\. Regular Bias and Accuracy Auditing

AI models drift. Training data becomes outdated. A model that performed well at deployment may produce different outputs six months later. FCA-compliant contact centres run scheduled audits of AI accuracy and bias, checking whether the AI is treating different customer segments consistently and whether its outputs remain aligned with regulatory requirements.

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
| Compliance Element | What It Requires | Why It Matters |
| Named accountability | Senior Manager owns AI risk | SM\&CR personal liability |
| Interaction logging | Full audit trail, retrievable | Consumer Duty evidence |
| Vulnerability detection | Escalation protocols built in | FCA vulnerable customer guidance |
| Explainability | Decision logic traceable | Regulatory scrutiny readiness |
| Bias auditing | Scheduled model reviews | Consistent customer outcomes |

The Mistakes That Create Compliance Risk

Most compliance failures in AI contact centres are not the result of bad intentions. They come from deployment decisions made without sufficient regulatory context. The most common patterns we see when advising financial services firms:

Deploying AI without a governance framework first. The technology goes live before anyone has defined who owns the risk, how interactions are reviewed, or what happens when the AI gets it wrong.

Treating AI as a cost-reduction tool rather than a customer-facing system. Firms that focus exclusively on handling time and deflection rates tend to underinvest in the compliance infrastructure that makes AI sustainable.

Assuming the vendor handles compliance. Technology vendors sell platforms. They do not design your governance framework, assign your SM\&CR accountability, or ensure your AI meets the FCA's vulnerable customer requirements. That responsibility sits with the firm.

No plan for model drift. AI that is not monitored will degrade. Firms that deploy and forget are building a compliance liability that grows quietly over time.

The part most firms miss: FCA compliance for AI is not a one-time implementation task. It is an ongoing operational responsibility that requires the same rigour as any other regulated activity.

Where to Start

For financial services firms at the beginning of their AI contact centre journey, the practical starting point is not technology selection. [It is governance design.](/advisory)

Before evaluating platforms or vendors, firms should be able to answer three questions:

Who is the named Senior Manager accountable for AI risk in the contact centre?

How will we evidence good customer outcomes under Consumer Duty for AI-handled interactions?

What is our escalation protocol for vulnerable customers identified by the AI?

If those three questions have clear answers, the technology selection conversation becomes significantly more straightforward. If they do not, deploying AI creates regulatory exposure regardless of which platform is chosen.

The firms getting this right are not necessarily the ones with the most sophisticated AI. They are the ones that treated compliance architecture as a prerequisite, not an afterthought.

Fortay Connect works with UK financial services firms to design and deploy AI contact centre solutions that are built for FCA compliance from day one, not retrofitted to it. If you are planning an AI deployment or reviewing your current setup, get your free technology audit now.

  
  

FAQs

1\. Does Consumer Duty apply to AI-handled customer interactions?

Yes. Consumer Duty applies to all customer interactions regardless of whether they are handled by a human or an AI. Firms must be able to demonstrate that AI-led contact centre interactions deliver good outcomes, particularly under the consumer support outcome.

2\. Who is accountable for AI failures in a financial services contact centre?

Under SM\&CR, a named Senior Manager must own accountability for each material risk area, including technology risk. If an AI system produces a harmful or incorrect outcome for a customer, that Senior Manager carries personal regulatory liability.

3\. What does the FCA require for vulnerable customer handling in AI contact centres?

The FCA's finalised guidance on vulnerable customers requires firms to identify vulnerability and respond appropriately. AI systems must be able to detect signs of vulnerability such as distress or financial difficulty and escalate to a human agent with documented protocols.

4\. Do AI contact centre systems need to be explainable to satisfy FCA requirements?

Yes. The FCA expects firms to be able to account for decisions made in customer interactions. AI systems operating as black boxes are incompatible with this. Compliance teams must be able to reconstruct the decision logic behind any AI-generated response when required.

5\. What is model drift and why does it matter for FCA compliance?

Model drift occurs when an AI system's outputs change over time as training data becomes outdated. For FCA compliance, this matters because a model that was compliant at deployment may produce biased or inaccurate outputs months later. Regular audits are required to detect and correct drift.

items.metaDescription: Stalling pipeline? Learn how conversational intelligence and AI sales tools help UK teams close deals faster, cut admin, and boost win rates by 30%+.
items.body:
If your pipeline is stalling, your reps are drowning in admin, and deals are taking longer to close than they should, the problem usually isn't effort. It's the absence of the right intelligence at the right moment.

According to [Bain & Company's 2025 analysis](https://www.cirrusinsight.com/blog/ai-in-sales), sales reps spend only 25% of their working hours actually selling. The rest goes to data entry, research, follow-ups, and reporting. That's a structural problem, and no amount of motivational training fixes it.

The good news: the gap between teams that close fast and teams that don't is increasingly a technology gap, not a talent gap. Here's how to close it.

Key stat: [ZoomInfo's 2025 State of AI report](https://www.cirrusinsight.com/blog/ai-in-sales) found that 81% of sales professionals using AI report shorter deal cycles, and 73% see larger deal sizes. These aren't marginal gains.

Key Takeaways

Sales reps spend only 25% of their time actually selling; AI can double that by automating admin

Conversational intelligence analyses every call, email, and meeting to surface real pipeline intelligence

69% of sellers using AI shortened their sales cycle by an average of one week (LinkedIn, 2025)

Real-time coaching, not post-mortem reviews, is what compresses the feedback loop and ramps reps faster

The 17-point revenue growth gap between AI-adopting and non-adopting teams compounds quickly in a tight market

Build a Pipeline That Actually Works

The sales pipeline isn't just a reporting tool. It's the architecture of your revenue. When it's poorly defined, every rep operates differently, opportunities fall through the gaps, and [forecasting becomes guesswork](https://www.fortayconnect.com/content/forecasting-tools-help-avoid-sales-inaccuracies).

A high-performing pipeline has three non-negotiable characteristics:

Visibility: Every deal has a clear status, owner, and next action. Nothing lives in someone's inbox or memory.

Focus: Resources concentrate on deals with the highest probability of closing, not the loudest stakeholder.

Consistency: Repeatable processes mean your best rep's playbook becomes everyone's playbook.

Where Most Pipelines Break Down

The common failure points aren't hard to spot once you know what to look for:

Manual CRM updates that lag behind reality, creating a pipeline view that's days out of date

Sales and marketing misalignment, where qualified leads arrive without context and warm prospects go cold

Untracked conversations, where a prospect expressed buying intent on a call but nobody logged it

These aren't process failures. They're information failures. And that's exactly where AI steps in.

How AI and Conversational Intelligence Accelerate Closures

Traditional sales forecasting relies on gut feel and what reps choose to log. [Conversational intelligence](https://www.fortayconnect.com/conversational-intelligence) changes the input entirely: instead of relying on self-reported data, it analyses every call, every email thread, every customer interaction to surface what's actually happening in your pipeline.

The practical impact is significant. [According to LinkedIn's 2025 research](https://www.cirrusinsight.com/blog/ai-in-sales), 69% of sellers using AI shortened their sales cycle by an average of one week. Across a full team and a full quarter, that compounds into a meaningful revenue advantage.

What Conversational Intelligence Actually Does

It's worth being specific here, because "AI in sales" gets used to describe everything from basic chatbots to sophisticated revenue intelligence platforms. Conversational intelligence operates at the conversation layer:

|  |  |
| :-: | :-: |
| Capability | What It Means in Practice |
| Real-time call analysis | Flags objections, competitor mentions, and sentiment shifts as they happen |
| Automated summaries | Generates call notes and next actions instantly, no manual logging |
| Deal risk alerts | Identifies deals going quiet or moving backwards before they stall |
| Coaching triggers | Surfaces specific moments from calls for targeted manager feedback |
| Predictive scoring | Ranks deals by close probability based on conversation signals, not rep opinion |

The Admin Problem, Solved

[Bain & Company found](https://www.cirrusinsight.com/blog/ai-in-sales) that AI can effectively double the proportion of time reps spend actually selling by automating the administrative layer. That's not a small efficiency gain. For a team of ten reps, recovering just one hour of selling time per day is the equivalent of adding two full-time salespeople. No extra headcount required.

Sales Acceleration Techniques That Actually Move Deals

Data and tools only create the conditions for faster closing. The techniques below are where that potential converts into revenue.

Real-Time Coaching, Not Post-Mortem Reviews

Most sales coaching happens too late: a manager reviews a lost deal weeks after it was winnable. Conversational intelligence flips this. Managers are alerted to at-risk deals in real time, can listen to specific call moments without sitting through the full recording, and can coach on the exact objection that's stalling progress.

The result is a compressed feedback loop. New reps ramp faster. Experienced reps refine their approach based on data, not instinct.

Value-Based Selling Over Feature Pitching

Deals stall when prospects can't connect your product to their specific business outcome. [Sales analytics](https://www.fortayconnect.com/content/ai-sales-analytics-trends-to-watch) tools now surface which talk tracks correlate with closed deals versus which ones produce long, inconclusive follow-up chains. That lets teams standardise around what actually wins, rather than what sounds good in a pitch meeting.

Follow-Up That Doesn't Drop the Ball

A significant proportion of deals are lost not because the prospect said no, but because follow-up was inconsistent. AI-driven CRM automation handles this: personalised nudges when engagement drops, multi-channel touchpoints timed to prospect behaviour, and content recommendations matched to where the buyer sits in their decision process.

"83% of sales teams using AI reported revenue growth, compared to just 66% of teams without it." — [Salesforce Research, 2024](https://www.cirrusinsight.com/blog/ai-in-sales)

That 17-percentage-point gap is the cost of not acting.

In Practice: How Barracuda Closed Faster With AI

Barracuda's sales team faced a familiar set of problems: manual note-taking eating into selling time, inconsistent onboarding for new reps, and follow-up that relied too heavily on individual discipline rather than systematic process.

After implementing Zoom Revenue Accelerator, the results were concrete:

2 hours saved per rep per day through automated call summaries and action item generation

Faster ramp time for new hires, using real call clips for targeted, asynchronous coaching

A culture of shared learning, where top-performer conversations became team-wide training material

The outcome wasn't just efficiency. Barracuda exceeded its business objectives and fundamentally changed how sales enablement worked across the team. Reps closed more deals, more quickly, with less administrative overhead dragging on their capacity.

This is what AI in sales looks like when it's implemented with a clear outcome in mind, rather than deployed as a technology experiment.

The Bottom Line

Closing sales deals faster isn't about pushing harder or adding more touchpoints. It's about removing the friction that slows your team down and replacing gut-feel decisions with real intelligence.

When your pipeline is structured, your reps are freed from admin, and your managers coach in real time rather than in retrospect, deal velocity follows naturally.

The teams pulling ahead right now aren't working longer hours. They're working with better information.

Ready to see what this looks like for your team? [Fortay Connect](https://www.fortayconnect.com/about-us) helps UK sales leaders implement [conversational intelligence](https://www.fortayconnect.com/conversational-intelligence) and [AI-driven revenue tools](https://www.fortayconnect.com/ai) that turn pipeline potential into closed deals. [Get in touch](https://www.fortayconnect.com/contact-us) to start the conversation.

FAQs

1\. How does conversational intelligence differ from traditional call recording?

Traditional call recording captures audio. Conversational intelligence analyses it, extracting sentiment, objections, competitor mentions, and buying signals in real time. The output isn't a playback file; it's actionable intelligence that feeds directly into coaching, forecasting, and deal management.

2\. What's the fastest way to implement AI sales tools in my team?

Start with a tool that integrates with your existing CRM and communications stack. Begin with call analysis and automated summaries before expanding to predictive scoring and full pipeline automation. Quick wins build the internal buy-in needed for broader adoption.

3\. Will AI replace my salespeople?

No. [Gartner predicts](https://www.gartner.com/) that 75% of B2B buyers will still prefer human interaction for high-stakes decisions by 2030. AI handles the repetitive and analytical work; your reps handle the relationships, negotiations, and complex closes that require genuine human judgement.

items.metaDescription: GoToConnect cloud-based telephony enables ESI Technologies to enhance customer service and workforce flexibility
items.body:
ESI Technologies

Established in 1919, ESI Technologies is a leading supplier of process equipment and engineering solutions for the biotech, pharmaceutical, chemical, food and energy industries in Ireland, UK and Benelux. It has plants in Cork and Cwmbran. [www.esitechgroup.com](http://www.esitechgroup.com)

Challenges

With pharmaceutical and biotech industries in Ireland growing strongly, and customers expecting greater speed and efficiency from suppliers, ESI Technologies was keen to increase the flexibility and responsiveness of its systems.

Alan Venner, IT Business Unit Leader at ESI Technologies, says: "Customers were increasingly using multiple online and mobile communication channels to contact us, and our existing hard-wired PBX phone system seemed inflexible and restrictive by comparison."

As part of a wider upgrade to its computer systems, which included switching to cloud-based platforms, ESI Technologies decided to review its phone system and explore VoIP options.

Alan explains: "Everything was up for grabs from an IT perspective. We looked at what sister companies were doing within the group and explored a number of suppliers. We knew about LogMeIn because we were already using GoToMeeting, so we set up a call to find out more about its cloud-based phone system, GoToConnect."

Solution

Following an initial proposal, LogMeIn introduced ESI Technologies to its local specialist unified communications and collaboration partner, Fortay Connect.

Mark Taylor from Fortay Connect says: "We matched the requirements and use cases of ESI Technology to the capabilities of GoToConnect. The company's call requirements were quite straightforward, but we were able to use the infinite flexibility of GoToConnect to create a bespoke set-up for their needs."

Alan adds: "We purchased 76 GoToConnect seats for our users in Ireland and Wales. The system was easy to set up and the onboarding ran smoothly, thanks to excellent planning and regular communication from the project team."

Results

Alan says: "The flexibility and customisation we now have at our fingertips is light years ahead of anything we had before. GoToConnect has really enhanced our capabilities, with features such as call groups, forwarding, caller ID and auto-attendant services."

Customers calling ESI Technologies now have many more options than simply leaving a voicemail. Calls not answered immediately are automatically forwarded to standby receptionists or mobile phones, enabling staff to receive and make calls wherever they are. These flexible call-routing capabilities have almost eliminated the problem of unanswered calls for ESI Technologies. All customer-facing product specialists now have the GoToConnect app on their mobiles, so they can always keep in touch with customers.

Alan adds: "When a customer has gone to the effort of calling us, rather than using emails or messaging, we want to ensure they're able to speak to somebody. GoToConnect allows us to provide that personal interaction almost every time. It gives us much greater flexibility by enabling our people to stay connected and work seamlessly from anywhere."

Testimonial

"LogMeIn offered the prestige, the reputation and the expertise we were looking for. We like to build partnerships with our suppliers, and LogMeIn aligned with that approach and had the technological back-up to support our long-term requirements"

items.metaDescription: The real Living Wage provides a voluntary benchmark for employers that wish to ensure their staff earn a wage they can live on, not just the government minimum.
items.body:
We are delighted to share that we are an accredited Living Wage Employer. This means that every member of staff working for Fortay Connect will earn above a real Living Wage. This commitment applies to not only directly employed staff but also to our third party contracted staff.

The real Living Wage is higher than the government's minimum, or National Living Wage, and is an independently calculated hourly rate of pay that is based on the actual cost of living.

It is calculated each year and is announced by the Living Wage Foundation as part of Living Wage Week. It is currently £9.90 in the UK, with a higher rate of £11.05 for London, reflecting the higher costs of living in the capital.

Katherine Chapman, Director, Living Wage Foundation said: "We're delighted that Fortay Connect has joined the movement of almost 9,000 responsible employers across the UK who voluntarily commit to go further than the government minimum to make sure all their staff earn enough to live on."

The real Living Wage provides a voluntary benchmark for employers that wish to ensure their staff earn a wage they can live on, not just the government minimum. Since 2011 the Living Wage movement has delivered a pay rise to over 300,000 people and put over £1.6 billion extra into the pockets of low paid workers.
